title: Discovery: Batching & Hosting Priorities - Quasar Retail Analytics
summary: Initial discovery to surface cost per token sensitivity, batching and KV/prefix cache expectations, and hosting preference tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated vs VPC private). Customer has a constrained budget for Q1 pilot and strict audit/residency needs for some datasets. They want a two-week benchmark pilot and pricing for a 3-month POC with clear pass/fail on latency and unit cost.

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2028-11-16
Start Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood CSM), Aisha Rahman (Quasar HoML), Tom Erickson (Quasar Platform), Diego Morales (Quasar SRE), Emma Li (Quasar Product)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect): Discussed per-token sensitivity, caching and batching levers; evaluated hosted vs dedicated vs private for compliance; agreed on pilot timeline and data artifacts to share.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Can we do quick intros and then jump into the bit about budget and latency?
[00:10] Aisha Rahman: Yeah hi, I'm Aisha, lead ML at Quasar. We're trying to replace a mixture of heuristics and slower transformer endpoints. Budget's tight.
[00:15] Tom Erickson: Tom here, platform. We're responsible for infra and security - VPC rules, egress, that sort of stuff.
[00:20] Priya Shah: Priya from Redwood, I focus on performance and benchmark decks.
[00:24] Diego Morales: Diego, SRE. We care about observability and audit logs.
[00:30] Liam Carter: Great. Very quickly, what's the approximate monthly token budget you have in mind for a pilot?
[00:36] Aisha Rahman: For Q1 pilot, we carved out about 5 million input tokens and 15 million output tokens per month, so roughly 20m tokens. It's more a gating exercise to see if unit economics work.
[00:48] Liam Carter: Understood. So that means per-token pricing and the batching/caching levers will determine whether hosted or dedicated makes sense. If cost per token on hosted is too high we can look at dedicated pools with reserved capacity.
[01:05] Emma Li: Our end-user latency bar is 400ms P95 for search rerank flows but for the chat assistants 800ms okay. So there's some wiggle room depending on use case.
[01:15] Priya Shah: That's good context. One thing we always surface: if you can batch at the request layer and use prefix/KV caching for common prompts you can reduce per-token compute significantly without impacting tail latency for non-cached requests.
[01:29] Tom Erickson: Can you explain prefix cache again? Sorry, sometimes the terms get swapped.
[01:33] Priya Shah: Sure—prefix cache stores the KV cache for common prompt prefixes so subsequent requests reuse the cached state and skip recomputation of earlier tokens. It helps when you have repeated beginning-of-conversation or repeated system prompts. It's not magic for totally unique prompts.
[01:45] Aisha Rahman: Our rerank pipeline has a lot of repeated prefix; we should get good wins there.
[01:49] Diego Morales: From a security side, we need SOC2 and ISO documents, plus proof of enclave or KMS integrations if we do private.
[01:57] Liam Carter: We have SOC2 Type II in our docs portal, and we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments; for hosted we offer at-rest encryption and restricted retention windows. We'll share the security pack.
[02:07] Emma Li: Is there a different price for VPC/private vs hosted?
[02:11] Liam Carter: Yes, typically private deployments (VPC or on-prem) carry a platform or seat fee plus reserved capacity pricing. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. Dedicated is in between—reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput.
[02:24] Aisha Rahman: Walk us through a concrete example: given our 20m tokens, what's the delta between hosted and dedicated?
[02:31] Priya Shah: I'll give a rough ballpark: hosted for a mid-sized Llama derivative at 16k context might be around X cents per output token in our public list—(note: numbers redacted in transcript) but with batching and prefix cache you can reduce effective per-output-token compute by 20-50% depending on cache hit rate. Dedicated can drop compute unit cost further because reserved GPUs amortize overhead and you can use aggressive quantization profiles.
[02:58] Tom Erickson: Aggressive quantization meaning 4-bit or 8-bit? How does that affect quality?
[03:03] Priya Shah: We support 8-bit and 4-bit-ish quantized runtimes; for many retrieval-augmented generation and classification tasks 8-bit maintains quality, 4-bit can be okay for some models but you'd want to validate on your eval sets. We'll recommend quant levels per model and workload.
[03:18] Aisha Rahman: Could you run a small conversion estimate—like, if we have 40% prefix cache hit and medium batching it lowers our tokens by what percent?
[03:27] Priya Shah: If 40% of requests hit prefix cache and those cached prefixes avoid recomputing ~30 tokens on average, that translates into roughly a 12% compute reduction. Add batching (if you can batch 3-4 requests) you might get another 10–20% efficiency. Combined, optimistic case maybe 25–30% unit cost reduction. Conservative maybe 10–15%.
[03:50] Liam Carter: Also note that batching helps throughput but can add a little tail latency; we can configure per-route latency SLOs so critical low-latency routes bypass batching or use micro-batches.
[04:00] Diego Morales: What's micro-batching?
[04:02] Priya Shah: Micro-batching bundles small numbers of concurrently in-flight requests to keep GPU utilization high but keeps batch sizes low so tail latencies remain acceptable.
[04:11] Tom Erickson: For networking, if we do VPC-private, will Redwood require peering or a private link? We need to avoid public egress unless we approve it.
[04:20] Liam Carter: For Private we do customer-managed VPC with private endpoints—no public egress. For Dedicated in hosted cloud we can do PrivateLink or VPN peering for enterprise customers. We'll document options.
[04:29] Emma Li: On pilots, what's a realistic timeline? We need results by end of Q1.
[04:34] Liam Carter: Two-week benchmark to validate latency and per-token numbers, then a 3-month pilot. So if we kick off bench late Nov, you'd have perf numbers mid-Dec and a pilot window in Jan–Mar.
[04:45] Aisha Rahman: Who runs the benchmark? We prefer Redwood to run with our prompts but we can grant access to some sample data.
[04:53] Priya Shah: We usually run a hybrid: customer provides prompt set and traffic distribution, Redwood runs server-side probes in a controlled environment (hosted/dedicated/private variants) and provides the result spreadsheets. We'll need sample prompts, sequence length histograms, and expected concurrency patterns.
[05:08] Tom Erickson: We'll try to provide histograms—our tail has some long sequences up to 3k tokens for full-context customer chat. Most are under 512.
[05:16] Priya Shah: That distribution matters a lot for kernel selection and batching profiles. If you have long tails, we might route those to a different pool optimized for long sequences.
[05:25] Aisha Rahman: How about cost modeling—do you do a spreadsheet that shows per-route routing and blended unit cost?
[05:31] Liam Carter: Yes we'll provide a unit-cost model that takes inputs: percent routed to low-latency pool, cache hit rate, avg tokens in/out, batching factor, reserved pool amortization. We can tailor it to your traffic mix.
[05:43] Diego Morales: On instrumentation, what telemetry do we get? Token-level cost breakdown? Trace spans?
[05:48] Marcus Lee: Marcus from CSM: we expose per-request token counts, latency histograms, and a cost breakdown per API key and model. We can add tracing hooks for our customers; you can forward spans to your observability backend.
[06:00] Emma Li: Do you give visibility into KV cache hit rates? That would help tuning.
[06:04] Priya Shah: Yes, we expose cache hit/miss metrics per route and per prefix key. Helps prioritize which prompts to canonicalize.
[06:12] Aisha Rahman: Are there any hard minimums for Dedicated? e.g., minimum GPUs or monthly commit?
[06:18] Liam Carter: For Dedicated there's typically a minimum monthly commitment tied to GPU pools—it's negotiable but most customers choose 1-2 GPU nodes minimum for production, smaller for dev. We'll share ranges in the SOW.
[06:29] Tom Erickson: Can Redwood support canary rollouts across model versions? We want to avoid regressions.
[06:33] Priya Shah: Yes, rollouts and automatic fallback policies are part of the console. You can run canaries, A/B, and configure automatic fallback to a cheaper model if quality drops or latency increases.
[06:44] Aisha Rahman: Okay re: quality—what's our fail criteria for the pilot? We were thinking: P95 latency must be under 400ms for rerank, unit cost below X (we'll specify) and no data exfil risk.
[06:55] Liam Carter: Sounds good. We'll codify pass/fail in the SOW.
[07:00] Diego Morales: On compliance, for the datasets we cannot leave region—some datasets must stay in EU. Does Redwood support region pins?
[07:07] Liam Carter: Yes, hosted regions and private deployments can be pinned. For highly sensitive data, Private in customer VPC or on-prem is the recommended path.
[07:16] Aisha Rahman: One more on batching—our front-end sends individual requests now. How much engineering effort to enable batching?
[07:22] Priya Shah: If you can do small changes to the gateway to aggregate concurrent requests, it's a few engineer-days depending on stack. Alternatively you can use Redwood SDK's batching helper or our sidecar proxy.
[07:33] Tom Erickson: Is there an SDK sidecar we can drop into our K8s cluster?
[07:36] Priya Shah: Yes, we provide a sidecar proxy that handles batching client-side and metrics. We'll share the repo link.
[07:42] Emma Li: Great. For quantization, do you recommend we retrain or fine-tune? We have a small in-house fine-tune for domain tokens.
[07:50] Priya Shah: Usually we recommend evaluating 8-bit first without re-training. If you have fine-tunes, sometimes post-training quantization works; other times you need a short calibration pass. We can advise after we see your model family.
[08:03] Aisha Rahman: Are the pricing deltas big enough that a small infra investment to support batching always makes sense?
[08:08] Priya Shah: Often yes—engineering effort upfront can cut run costs meaningfully for high-volume paths. But if you have very sensitive latency paths, you may choose to bypass batching there. It's about routing and priorities.
[08:20] Liam Carter: Anything else on compliance or legal we should know?
[08:23] Tom Erickson: We'll need to vet the data processing addendum, SCCs for EU data, and support for customer KMS.
[08:30] Liam Carter: We'll include those in the security pack we send.
[08:34] Aisha Rahman: For the two-week bench, what access do you need?
[08:37] Priya Shah: Ideally an API key or a temporary dataset + prompt set. If you prefer we can run within your VPC via private connectors. For the hosted benchmark we usually run in our environment with your prompts; for private we'd run inside your network.
[08:50] Diego Morales: I'd prefer the VPC option for anything with PII.
[08:53] Liam Carter: Noted. We'll plan for a VPC connector for sensitive prompts.
[08:58] Emma Li: Can you also show different routing mixes in the cost model—like 70% hosted, 30% dedicated, or 100% dedicated?
[09:05] Liam Carter: Yes, we'll provide blended scenarios.
[09:08] Aisha Rahman: What's the expected variance in per-token cost month-to-month? We need predictability.
[09:13] Marcus Lee: With Dedicated reserved capacity you get much more predictable unit economics month-to-month. Hosted can vary with usage; we provide forecast tools and committed discounts for steady usage.
[09:24] Tom Erickson: For the POC, can Redwood instrument our observability stack with cost per trace?
[09:29] Marcus Lee: We can emit attributes for cost per request so you can join in your traces.
[09:33] Aisha Rahman: Any gotchas we should be aware of?
[09:36] Priya Shah: Watch out for tail sequences—they can bloat cost if routed to generic pools. Also, if you enable large batch windows indiscriminately you can regress tail latency. Canonicalizing prompts and using prefix cache tends to be low-effort, high-return.
[09:49] Diego Morales: Are there throttles or rate limits we should know?
[09:52] Liam Carter: We'll configure rate limits per-route and per-key to match your traffic; for Dedicated we'll provision capacity to hit your RPS targets.
[09:59] Emma Li: Ok let's recap and close with action items.
[10:02] Liam Carter: Recap: Quasar will share prompt set and histograms; Redwood will send pilot SOW + pricing; we'll schedule benchmark kickoff week of 11/27; security pack and region pins will be included.
[10:15] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good.
[10:17] Tom Erickson: Thanks everyone.
[10:20] Liam Carter: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with links.

End of transcript
questions: What are the expected engineering changes to support batching?
How will prefix cache affect our rerank flow?
What documentation is provided for SOC2/KMS integration?
